slides.sub: You may listen privately, and stop at any time
slides.title: Room 2: Sex
slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson 7. This is a lesson about intimacy in marriage, and I want to begin by saying that you may listen privately, and you may stop at any time.

slides.quote: “The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”
slides.narration:
Let’s begin with Scripture. First Corinthians chapter 7, verses 3 to 5.

“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”

slides.title: Written to married people
body: Paul answers questions the church had asked him. These words are about marriage. For you, engaged, they shape how you prepare.
slides.narration: Let me say first what this passage is. Paul is writing to married people in Corinth, answering questions the church had asked him. These words are about marriage. For you, engaged, they shape how you prepare and what you are preparing for.

slides.title: Almost everything is said twice
body: The husband, and likewise the wife. Paul speaks to both spouses in the same terms, with the same weight.
slides.narration: Now notice how the passage is built. Almost everything in it is said twice. The husband, and likewise the wife. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Paul speaks to both spouses, in the same terms, with the same weight. In many settings of his day, duties in marriage were commonly described from the husband’s side. Here Paul describes them from both.

slides.title: A responsibility of love, in both directions
body: Neither spouse is presented only as a person who may demand. Both are called to give, to care and to act with mutual honour.
slides.narration: Notice what Paul is doing. He addresses each spouse’s responsibility to the other. Neither spouse is presented only as a person who may demand. Both are called to give, to care and to act with mutual honour. The older translation “conjugal rights” can sound as if one person holds a claim over the other. Hear it in Paul’s own frame: a responsibility of love, in both directions.

slides.kicker: The line that is easiest to miss
slides.title: “Except perhaps by agreement”
body: Nothing here gives either spouse permission to use force, threats or pressure.
slides.sub: In marriage, intimacy is mutual, and freely given.
slides.narration:
And notice the line that is easiest to miss. When Paul speaks of abstaining for a time, he requires agreement: “except perhaps by agreement.” That reinforces the mutual pattern running through the passage. Nothing here gives either spouse permission to use force, threats or pressure.

That is the truth this lesson stands on. In marriage, intimacy is mutual. Mutual honour, mutual love, and freely given.

slides.title: Not ownership
body: Marriage does not give either spouse ownership of the other’s body in a way that removes consent. This passage cannot justify coercion.
slides.narration: That has sometimes been taught badly. The idea that “each belongs to the other” has occasionally been used as a claim of entitlement, and that reading has done real damage in Christian marriages. So let me say it plainly. Marriage does not give either spouse ownership of the other’s body in the sense of removing consent. This passage cannot justify coercion. It is about each person’s responsibilities in love, not a method of claiming access to a body against that person’s will.

slides.note: Consent must be freely given, and it can be withdrawn at any time. Silence, a previous yes, or the marriage itself is not continuing permission. A “no” must be safe in your marriage. If it is not, that needs help from outside the two of you.
slides.narration: Consent must be freely given, and it can be withdrawn at any time. Silence, a previous yes, or the marriage itself is not continuing permission. And a “no” must be safe in your marriage. If it is not, that is not a difference of expectation. It is something else, and it needs help from outside the two of you.

slides.title: Honour, love, and intimacy freely given
body: The rest is preparation for that.
slides.narration: That is the positive centre of this lesson: honour, love, and intimacy freely given. The rest is preparation for that.

slides.title: Everything discussed but this
body: Couples discuss the venue, the finances and where they will live, and say almost nothing about intimacy.
slides.narration:
So what usually goes wrong?

The first is silence. Some couples have been taught, rightly, to reserve sex for marriage. Almost none were taught how to talk about it beforehand. So they arrive at the wedding having thoroughly discussed the venue, the finances and where they will live, and having said almost nothing about intimacy.

slides.title: Guilty for having questions
body: A voice says a good Christian shouldn’t even be thinking about this. So people hold expectations while feeling guilty for having questions.
slides.narration: The second is shame about the questions themselves. Someone has real questions about desire, their body, their history or their fears, and cannot ask them, because a voice says a good Christian shouldn’t even be thinking about this. That produces a lonely position: holding expectations while feeling guilty for having questions.

slides.title: Strong feelings, different expectations
body: About affection, initiation, frequency and boundaries. And imported expectations from films, friends, pornography and novels.
slides.narration:
The third is mistaking attraction for preparation. A couple can have strong feelings and completely different expectations about affection, initiation, frequency and boundaries. Feelings tell you almost nothing about those.

The fourth is imported expectations, from films, from friends, from pornography, from romantic novels. Most people do not know they are carrying them until reality contradicts them.

slides.title: “It will all happen naturally”
body: The wedding changes the relationship’s commitments. It does not make comfort, confidence or shared desire automatic.
slides.narration: And the largest misconception of all: “Once we’re married, it will all happen naturally.” Within the Christian understanding used in this course, the wedding changes the relationship’s commitments. It does not make comfort, confidence or shared desire automatic.

slides.title: What did you learn about this subject growing up, from your family, your church or your friends?
body: Take a moment before you go on.
slides.narration: Pause here. What did you learn about this subject growing up, from your family, your church or your friends? Take a moment before you go on.

slides.title: No one should be shamed
body: Some have waited. Some carry previous experiences. Some carry experiences they did not choose.
slides.sub: This is not an interrogation. It is a conversation about what you were taught, believe and expect.
slides.narration: Different histories bring different questions. Some of you have waited. Some carry previous experiences. Some carry experiences you did not choose. No one should be shamed or treated as less worthy of love. This is not an interrogation about what either of you has done. It is a conversation about what you were taught, what you believe, what you expect and how you will speak to one another.

list: What did my family and church teach me about sex?
How will we tell each other what is comfortable, uncomfortable, too much?
What will we do when our desire is different?
How will we respond when one of us says no?
slides.narration: Here are the kinds of questions that help. What did my family teach me about sex, and what did my church teach me, often by implication rather than instruction? Those messages are still operating. What am I nervous about? What am I afraid might happen? That is often more revealing than asking what someone wants. How will we tell each other what feels comfortable, what is uncomfortable, what is too much? You need actual words for this. Mind-reading will not develop on its own. What will we do when our desire is different? Not if. When. And how will we respond when one of us says no?

slides.title: The wedding night is not an examination
body: You may be exhausted, nervous, laugh, or need to stop. None of that means anything is wrong. It is the beginning of learning each other.
slides.narration: Take the pressure off the wedding night. Films have trained us to expect something effortless and unforgettable. The reality is often less cinematic. You may be exhausted. You may be nervous. You may laugh. You may need to stop. None of that means anything is wrong with your marriage. The wedding night is the beginning of learning each other. It is not an examination. And the first months will have a learning curve, because there is one. Do not turn your first experiences into a verdict on your marriage.

list: “I’m not in the mood tonight, but I want to be close to you.”
slides.note: You do not owe affection, an alternative or an explanation to make a no valid.
slides.narration: What you need is the ability to say, without drama, “Can we try that differently?” “I like this.” “I’m not comfortable with that.” “I need more time.” And, “I’m not in the mood tonight, but I want to be close to you.” That last one is optional. You do not owe affection, an alternative or an immediate explanation to make a no valid. When it feels safe, a later conversation may help you understand and care for one another.

slides.kicker: A few plain words about health
slides.title: Pain is a reason to stop
body: If intimacy is painful or difficult, speak with a qualified healthcare professional.
slides.sub: Before marriage, ask a healthcare professional about sexual health testing, contraception and any medication concerns.
slides.narration: A few plain words about health. Pain is a reason to stop, not a test of commitment. If intimacy is painful or remains difficult, speak with a qualified healthcare professional rather than trying to endure it. Before marriage, ask a healthcare professional about sexual health testing, contraception and any medication concerns. That is preparation, not accusation.

slides.kicker: Matters that need their own care
body: Pornography does not place anyone beyond grace, but marriage will not resolve it. Painful experiences do not reduce your worth. A boundary is never something to overcome by pressure.
slides.narration: A few matters need their own care, and the worksheet gives them fuller attention. Pornography does not place anyone beyond grace, but marriage will not resolve it. An active or concealed pattern needs honest attention, accountability and appropriate help, and it may be wise to postpone marriage while it is being addressed. If painful experiences still affect you, what happened to you does not reduce your worth or make you unworthy of love. You may still need time, care and wise support when deciding whether you are ready for marriage. And a boundary is never something to overcome by pressure.

slides.title: About twenty minutes
list: What did I learn about sex growing up?
Which of those messages do I still believe?
What am I afraid you will expect of me?
slides.sub: You do not have to write anything down.
slides.narration: Your step has two parts. First, spend about twenty minutes alone with the questions in the worksheet. What did I learn about sex growing up? Was it spoken about, or only implied? What did I come to believe was shameful? Which of those messages do I still believe, and which do I want to leave behind? What do I think sex is for within marriage? What am I nervous about? What am I afraid you will expect of me? You do not have to write anything down.

slides.title: 45 to 60 minutes, in private
body: Either of you may stop at any time. Go slowly through what you were taught, what you believe now, and what you are nervous about.
slides.narration: Then set aside 45 to 60 minutes, in a private place, when neither of you is tired. Have your Lesson 2 rules in front of you. Either of you may stop at any time. Go slowly through what you were taught, what you believe now, and what you are nervous about. This is the part where couples go quiet, and the silence is usually not because there is nothing to say.

slides.title: A no is always respected
body: How you will tell each other what you want, and what you do not. A no will never be punished.
slides.sub: Record one agreement, and one matter to return to or seek help with.
slides.narration: Then agree together how you will tell each other what you want, and what you do not. And agree that a no will always be respected and never punished. Record one agreement, and one matter you will return to or seek help with.

body: “Is there anything about my history, my struggles or my expectations that you need to know before we marry?”
slides.note: You do not owe graphic details, or an account of experiences you did not choose. Share what is relevant, at a pace you control.
slides.narration: Finally, if you both feel able, each answer one question: “Is there anything about my history, my struggles or my expectations that you need to know before we marry?” You do not owe graphic details, and you do not owe an account of experiences you did not choose. Share what is relevant to health, consent, current commitments and expectations, at a pace you control. If something difficult comes out, listen without pressing for details. Thank the person, ask what support they want, and allow time before you respond further.

slides.title: Words only
body: This conversation uses words only. Nothing in it asks you to do anything physical.
slides.narration: This conversation uses words only. Nothing in it asks you to do anything physical.

body: Lord, You made us for love, and You call us to honour. Keep us from shame, and keep us from pressure. Give us words to speak with honesty and patience. Where we are afraid, give us courage. Where we carry pain, give us care. Make our marriage a place where a “no” is safe and a “yes” is freely given. Amen.
slides.narration:
Let me close with a short prayer.

Lord, You made us for love, and You call us to honour. Keep us from shame, and keep us from pressure. Give us words to speak with honesty and patience. Where we are afraid, give us courage. Where we carry pain, give us care. Make our marriage a place where a “no” is safe and a “yes” is freely given. Amen.

slides.title: Lesson 8
slides.narration: I’ll see you in Lesson 8.
